newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Analysts divided over Bank Austria share issue.
newsitem.headline: Analysts divided over Bank Austria share issue.

text.p: Bank Austria will announce the issue price for a three billion schillings preference share issue later this week, with analysts divided on the project's chances of success.

A spokesman for the nation's biggest bank said it would release the price for the 9-23 June issue on Thursday afternoon or early on Friday. Analysts forecast a small discount to Wednesday's close of 424 schillings.
The Bank Austria spokesman ruled out any news on an eagerly awaited exchange offer to Creditanstalt shareholders, however.
"The share exchange ratio will probably not be made public until the second half of June," he said, contradicting earlier statements by Bank Austria chief executive Gerhard Randa.

Randa had expressed the hope that the capital increase would coincide with an agreement on the share exchange. Bank Austria undertook to offer its shares to Creditanstalt investors when it took control of its former rival in January.
Austrian banking analysts were disappointed that the capital increase would go ahead without a clear indication of the share swap ratio.
Some also raised doubts that there would be a stampede of buyers, despite a cheap price/earnings ratio of below 10.

"Regardless of the price, I do not think it will be a particularly attractive issue," said a Vienna-based analyst, adding that political infighting over the state-owned bank did little to instil investor confidence.

Bank Austria's management and Vienna's ruling Social Democrats this week rejected allegations they hushed up a 1995 deal that gave Germany's Westdeutsche Landesbank Zentrale WDLg.D first refusal on a controlling stake.

Conservative Economy Minister Hannes Farnleitner, outraged at news of WestLB's first option on the shares, has called on the Social Democrat-led national government to respond by annulling Bank Austria's acquisition of Creditanstalt.
One international analyst foresaw few difficulties in placing Bank Austria preference shares but added the longer term outlook for the stock was bleak, given the prevailing political uncertainty.
"I doubt the share price will firm afterwards," he said.
Other experts painted a more positive picture, however. They saw a bank with immense potential to slim down its operations and increase profit margins following its takeover of Creditanstalt.
"If one ignores all the emotion that Austria's closed banking scene evokes, one sees that this issue has a certain charm and ought to appeal to international investors," said a Vienna-based analyst.
